<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and format-compliant (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structures on both sides), so the decision turns on which live route survived best. PRO's core route — the "Buy" button mismatch plus the platform windfall, cured by a single supervised transfer that the seller cannot draft away — was never squarely neutralized. PRO defused CON's strongest early lines: the replication fear was answered with the "one licence, one successor account, every generation" rule (and CON's own admission that PRO's rule delivers only one copy to one relative actually confirms rather than refutes the modesty of the grant); the subscription-flight threat was turned effectively ("music and film moved to streaming with no inheritance law anywhere"); and the privacy attack was met with the strong observation that the status quo leaves the shameful reading history with a corporation anyway, and that paper shelves and diaries already pass by default. PRO also handled CON's best dilemma (waivable = mere default term; unwaivable = compulsory family disclosure) with a coherent distinction between a rule non-waivable by boilerplate and one the testator may still override — "a floor; a label is a menu the seller writes" was the cleanest comparative line in the debate. CON's best material — upstream sublicensing constraints, the perpetual heirship bureaucracy, and the closing reframe that portable files give ownership you can hold while a heritable licence is "a better-worded dependency" — is genuinely good and partially survives PRO's "that's between the platform and its publishers" answer, which is more allocation-by-assertion than refutation. But CON never defended the windfall PRO put at the centre, and its eventual answer (restitution/refunds) was visibly weak; CON's late claim that PRO's rule binds only future sales was asserted in the closing without support and after PRO could respond, which limits its credit. Net: PRO made the decisive clash easier to resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing hit on CON's restitution answer: asked what the family of a man who already spent thousands gets, CON offered "a refund, a claim, damages" and called settlement "cheaper for platforms" — PRO's image of a widow litigating a Kindle library title by title, and the line that "a remedy designed to be cheaper for the party that wrote the misleading word is not a remedy," converted CON's own concession into proof of the windfall CON had never defended.</best_rebuttal>
